topic: laying a three-strand hemp rope on an old ropewalk and balancing twist against closing

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: miernik naciagu pozyczony ze stoczni

base: I am laying a three-strand hemp rope on an old ropewalk behind the village hall.
An old mooring line hangs from the beam there, laid tight and still perfectly sound.
I borrowed a tension gauge from the boatyard, since guessing the pull always ruined my strands.
My first attempt kinked badly as soon as I took the strain off it.
Should I spin the yarns harder, or is the fault in how I close the rope?
The fault lies in the closing, because a kink means the strands hold more twist than the rope.
Every yarn must be spun one way and the strands laid firmly the other.
Balance between those two twists is what keeps a finished rope lying quiet.
Take the strain off slowly, and watch whether the rope wants to writhe.
I spun the yarns more evenly and laid the strands with a steadier hand.
The tension gauge held near forty pounds through the whole length this time.
The rope still writhes a little, though far less than it did before.
Do I add more turns at the top, or fewer when closing the rope?
Take turns out of the closing, since the strands are plainly carrying enough twist already.
A rope that writhes has been closed too hard against the twist in its strands.
Slack the top by a quarter turn for every fathom of finished length.
Run the traveller down slowly and let each yard settle before you go further.
I slacked the top as you said and the rope now lies almost dead straight.
The tension gauge stayed steady and the strands closed without any sign of writhing.
That old mooring line on the beam feels much harder and stiffer than mine.
Is that hardness a virtue, or does a softer rope serve better in use?
Hardness suits a mooring, because a stiff rope resists chafe where it crosses a fairlead.
Tar adds much of that stiffness and keeps the fibres from taking up water.
A softer lay runs better through blocks and holds a knot far more kindly.
Decide what the rope must do before you decide how hard to close it.
I want the rope for hauling hay bales up into the loft each summer.
It will run over a wooden sheave and be knotted twenty times a day.
The lay I have made feels softer than the line hanging on the beam.
Should I tar it anyway, or leave the hemp bare for indoor work?
Leave it bare, because tar stiffens a rope you will be knotting all day.
Indoors there is no salt and very little damp to rot the fibres.
Bare hemp also grips a wooden sheave better than a tarred rope ever will.
Whip both ends properly and the rope will outlast the loft it serves.
I whipped both ends with waxed twine and hung the rope in the loft.
It runs sweetly over the sheave and takes a bowline without any fuss.
After a fortnight of hauling it has stretched by nearly half a fathom.
Is that stretch a sign of weakness, or simply the rope bedding down?
That is the rope bedding down, and every new hemp line does exactly the same.
Constructional stretch pulls the yarns close together and finishes within the first month.
Shorten the eye once it has settled, rather than fighting the stretch now.
After that the length will hold steady for many seasons of ordinary work.
